name: Yuzu extract

lead: Yuzu is a tart citrus fruit grown mainly in Japan and Korea, and extracts of its peel, juice or seed appear in some Asian skin-care products for their vitamin C and polyphenol content. People use it for brighter, more even skin tone.

The chain is antioxidant and pigment: in cell studies a yuzu seed compound, nomilin, showed antioxidant activity and lowered melanin production in cultured melanoma cells, pointing to less pigment and a more even tone. Published work is laboratory and animal studies; human skin trials were not found.

paras: Used in serums, creams, masks and toners as a brightening step, typically in a morning and evening routine paired with sunscreen, which tone-evening depends on. Users generally look for changes over several weeks.
No specific safety data for cosmetic use were found; citrus ingredients can irritate or sensitise some skin. A patch test is the usual precaution.

angle.text: Yuzu extract is used in Asian skincare as a vitamin C and polyphenol botanical for brighter, more even skin tone. A yuzu seed compound showed antioxidant activity and lowered melanin production in cell studies, which is the route to less pigment.

lead: Yuzu (Citrus junos) is a tart, aromatic citrus fruit believed to have originated in central China and now grown mainly in Japan and Korea.[1] Extracts of the peel, juice or seed appear in some Asian skin-care products, usually marketed for their vitamin C and polyphenol content, with the aim of brighter, more even-looking skin.[2]

In the laboratory, a seed compound called nomilin has been reported to inhibit tyrosinase, the enzyme at the start of melanin production, and to lower pigment-related proteins in cultured mouse melanoma cells; this is the main basis for yuzu's use in brightening products.[2] Other published work on yuzu extract concerns antiplatelet, glucose and cognition-related effects in cells and animals.[3][4][5]
No human trial of yuzu extract for skin appearance was found.
infobox: Central China; introduced to Japan and Korea in the Tang dynasty[1]
Vitamin C, hesperidin, naringin, limonoids such as nomilin[2][3]

paras: Wikipedia describes yuzu as a citrus hybrid in the Rutaceae family that grew wild in Tibet and central China and was introduced to Japan and Korea during the Tang dynasty. The fruit is tart and fragrant, resembling grapefruit with mandarin-like overtones, and the tree is slow to bear fruit and relatively frost-hardy for a citrus.[1]

In Japan the zest and juice are used like lemons in ponzu, yuzu kosho and tea; in Korea it appears in yuja-cheong and yuja tea. Peel oil is marketed as a fragrance, with the compound yuzunone contributing to its aroma.[1] A Japanese custom, the winter-solstice yuzu bath (Toji), floats whole fruits or halves in hot water; the custom dates to at least the early 18th century and is said to soften skin and relax the mind.[1] This bathing tradition is a cultural link between yuzu and skin care. Japan's domestic production was about 27,000 tons in 2016.[1]

A 2022 study reported that nomilin from yuzu seed had antioxidant activity and reduced melanin production in cultured mouse B16F10 melanoma cells. Nomilin was identified from the limonoid glucoside fraction of the seed husk as a previously unknown tyrosinase inhibitor, acted as a noncompetitive inhibitor in assays, and suppressed protein expression of tyrosinase, TRP-1, TRP-2 and MITF in a concentration-dependent manner at non-toxic concentrations below 100 micrograms per millilitre, with reduced phosphorylation of PKA and CREB. The authors describe yuzu peel and seed as rich in vitamin C, citric acid and polyphenols.[2]

Methanolic and ethanolic yuzu extracts and their components hesperidin and naringin inhibited platelet aggregation in rat and human blood samples; the oral extract or hesperidin prolonged mouse tail bleeding time, and the human-blood study linked the effect to PLC-gamma and Akt signalling, thromboxane formation and granule secretion.[3][4] A rat study found that long-term oral yuzu extract (3% of diet) prevented beta-amyloid accumulation and cognitive dysfunction in a beta-amyloid infusion model.[5]

No studies found on yuzu extract for skin. Registered human trials of citron (Citrus junos) peel extract concern blood cholesterol (a 70-person study begun in 2017), and a 40-person supplement trial in perimenopausal symptoms begun in 2023 is listed.[6][7] The pigment and antioxidant findings above come from cell and animal work.
No specific safety data for cosmetic use of yuzu extract were found. Citrus-derived ingredients can irritate or sensitise some skin in general.
